title: Jupiter Has Its Own, Busier Way of Blocking the Solar Wind
summary: NASA's Juno spacecraft found that Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, blocks the solar wind in a much more complex way than Earth does. This research was led by scientists at the University of Iowa. The Sun constantly sends out the solar wind, and when it reaches a planet with a magnetic field, it meets a boundary called the bow shock. At Earth, this boundary slows and heats the particles, sends most of the solar wind around the planet, and keeps harmful particles from our air. Jupiter also has a bow shock, but it uses plasma waves with many frequencies, called harmonics, to slow and heat the particles. It is a bit like music: several notes together sound richer than one. Jupiter also has smaller shocks called shocklets that slow the solar wind before the main bow shock. Earth mostly uses its main bow shock alone, because the impact there is not as powerful, said Bill Kurth, an Iowa scientist on the Juno mission since 2011. The results could help scientists understand huge shock waves from exploding stars.
why_it_matters: Learning how planets shield themselves helps you understand the invisible forces that protect Earth, a bit like a shield protecting you on a windy day.

An invisible force around a planet that can push back against charged particles from space.
A boundary where the solar wind slows down and heats up when it meets a planet's magnetic field.

The Hubble telescope

questions.question: What is the solar wind?
options: Light from exploding stars
Rain falling on Jupiter
Wind blowing across Jupiter's clouds
A stream of particles constantly sent out by the Sun

questions.question: What does the bow shock do at Earth?
options: It stops the Sun from shining
It makes Jupiter's clouds spin
It slows and heats the particles and sends most of the solar wind around the planet
It pulls the solar wind into the planet
questions.correct_answer: It slows and heats the particles and sends most of the solar wind around the planet

questions.question: How is Jupiter's bow shock different from Earth's?
options: It uses plasma waves with many frequencies, called harmonics
It only works at night
It sends the solar wind straight through the planet
It has no bow shock at all
questions.correct_answer: It uses plasma waves with many frequencies, called harmonics

questions.question: What are shocklets?
options: Harmful particles in Earth's air
Tiny moons around Jupiter
Smaller shocks that slow the solar wind before the main bow shock
Musical notes played by Juno
questions.correct_answer: Smaller shocks that slow the solar wind before the main bow shock

questions.question: Why does Earth mostly use its main bow shock alone?
options: Because the Sun never sends wind toward Earth
Because the impact there is not as powerful
Because Earth has no magnetic field
Because Jupiter blocks the wind first
questions.correct_answer: Because the impact there is not as powerful

background_read: The Sun constantly sends out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind.
When this wind reaches a planet with a magnetic field, it meets a boundary called the bow shock, which slows and heats the particles and sends most of the wind around the planet.
Jupiter's bow shock works in a busier way than Earth's, using many plasma waves and smaller shocks called shocklets to slow the wind before the main boundary.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at the University of Iowa, using NASA's Juno spacecraft, including Bill Kurth.
WHAT: They found Jupiter blocks the solar wind in a more complex way than Earth, using plasma waves and smaller shocklets.
WHERE: At Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, at its bow shock.
WHY: To understand how planets shield themselves from the solar wind and how huge shock waves from exploding stars work.

perspectives.description: Kurth says Earth mostly uses its main bow shock alone, because the impact there is not as powerful as at Jupiter.
